10.7. Certified Bounds and Models🔗

The exponential in the figure returns us to the heat profile that opened the chapter. Here the question is quantitative: how far can a polynomial lie from the function anywhere on the stated interval? Increasing the degree can reduce that error, but the final zero-width band replaces the polynomial by the exponential itself: the same inequality with the exponential as its own model and error zero. The plotted coordinates illustrate the estimate; the certificates supply proofs.

The shared semantic vocabulary is intentionally small:

  • ApproxOn f g s ε means \lVert f(x)-g(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon for every x\in s;

  • BoundOn f s c means f(x)\leq c throughout s;

  • EnclosedOn f s lo hi means \mathrm{lo}\leq f(x)\leq\mathrm{hi} throughout s;

  • ResidualBound r s ε means \lVert r(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon throughout s.

These are ordinary propositions in the language of approximation theory. The certificate records ApproxCert, ResidualCert, BoundCert, and EnclosureCert store the functions, domain, and numerical data of one of them together with a sound field proving it; a QuadratureCert does the same for the error of an interval integral. Checked certificates compose through ordinary Lean theorems.

illustrates the complete exact path. The parser first turns the ordinary notation into an expression tree. Inspecting the logarithm records a nonzero condition on its argument. The differentiator constructs the candidate 1/x, and the analytic differentiation theorem justifies the ordinary statement that the derivative of \log at x is 1/x, provided x\ne0.

The condition printed by the inspection command is part of the answer. To use the derivative at a particular point, a theorem-facing tactic must prove that condition from the hypotheses. This is the same obligation that appeared in the affine Burgers denominator and in the logarithmic fundamental solution away from its pole. Polynomial examples need no such exclusion, but they pass through the same proof interface.

A CEGA query follows the same architecture but ends in a quantitative certificate. For

the parser again produces an expression tree, and a rational interval evaluator constructs candidate endpoints. A successful computation returns those endpoints together with a proof that every value on the input interval lies between them.

Taylor models use enclosures to bound their remainders while retaining polynomial structure. Derivative bounds also help determine a sufficient subdivision for quadrature.

10.7.2. Certified Approximation and Enclosures🔗

FloatLib supplies the interval arithmetic and elementary-function enclosures. The rational backend uses FloatLib.Numerics.Interval ℚ; PDEAtlas's RationalInterval extends it with just the endpoint-order proof hle. Its endpoints remain exact rationals. FloatLib's generic expression evaluator accepts CAS expressions through a proved semantic translation, and its upstream backends choose the endpoint representation and rounding policy. CEGA connects their containment proofs to real inequalities, so an analytic theorem can use a different representation without changing its statement.

The four basic certificate shapes.

On a domain s, the records name their data as follows: ApproxCert α E s has functions lhs and rhs and an error eps; ResidualCert α E s has a residual and an eps; BoundCert α s has a real function fn and an upper endpoint; EnclosureCert α s has fn, lo, and hi. Each sound field proves the corresponding proposition on s. These general records may contain noncomputable real data, while concrete rational enclosures provide executable endpoints. For example, an enclosure -0.01\le r(x)\le0.01 immediately gives a residual certificate with error 0.01; an enclosure of f-g inside [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon] gives an approximation certificate from f to g.

An approximation certificate stores two functions, an explicit domain and uniform error budget, and a proof of the corresponding norm bound. Exact equality is the zero-error special case. The budget is stored as a real number.

Its theorem-facing field is exactly

\operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon) \;:\!\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall x\in s,\quad \lVert f(x)-g(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

    A checked uniform approximation certificate on a domain.

    The fields lhs, rhs, and eps make the certificate composable as data, and sound proves the ApproxOn proposition. The budget is necessarily nonnegative on every nonempty domain; equivalently, a negative budget certifies only an empty domain.

    Fields

    lhs : α → E

    Left-hand function.

    rhs : α → E

    Right-hand/reference function.

    eps : ℝ

    Uniform error budget. It is nonnegative whenever s is nonempty.

    sound : CAS.Certificate.ApproxOn self.lhs self.rhs s self.eps

    lhs is uniformly eps-close to rhs on s.

An approximation or residual certificate has a nonnegative error budget unless its certified domain is empty. Equivalently, a negative budget can never be used to establish a nonvacuous estimate.

For either certificate family,

0\leq c.\mathrm{eps}\quad\lor\quad s=\varnothing.

Proof for Theorem 10.37
uses 0

If the domain is nonempty, choose one point in it. Soundness bounds a norm, which is nonnegative, by the stored budget; hence the budget is nonnegative by transitivity. If no point exists, the alternative s=\varnothing holds.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Approximation certificates compose by adding error budgets, pass through Lipschitz maps, and recover exact equality when the final budget is zero.

The three principal rules are

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon_1) \land\operatorname{ApproxOn}(g,h,s,\varepsilon_2) &\Longrightarrow \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,h,s,\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2),\\ \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,\varepsilon) \land L\geq0 \land\left(\forall u,v,\ \lVert\phi(u)-\phi(v)\rVert\leq L\lVert u-v\rVert\right) &\Longrightarrow \operatorname{ApproxOn}(\phi\circ f,\phi\circ g,s,L\varepsilon),\\ \operatorname{ApproxOn}(f,g,s,0) &\Longrightarrow f= g\quad\text{on }s. \end{aligned}

A real interval implementation supplies lower and upper endpoints, a membership predicate, and proofs that membership implies the corresponding real inequalities. Exact rational intervals are the registered instance; a verified finite-precision representation with the same two proofs feeds the same enclosure theorems.

Every backend instance must establish

x\in_{\!B} I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{lo}(I)\leq x\leq\operatorname{hi}(I).

The representation of I and the implementation of membership are otherwise abstract. For the rational backend, CEGA's endpoint inequalities are equivalent to FloatLib's real containment predicate. Attaching hle preserves that predicate and gives refinement and quadrature an ordered interval with a nonnegative radius.

Before interval compilation, an intrinsic syntax check rejects malformed rational literals whose denominator is zero. Division, logarithm, and square root remain ordinary real expressions with pointwise analytic validity conditions; this check handles only malformed syntax, so it cannot be bypassed by evaluating over an empty domain.

The nontrivial recursive clauses are

\begin{aligned} \operatorname{WF}(\operatorname{rat}(m,d))&\Longleftrightarrow d\neq0,\\ \operatorname{WF}(e_1\mathbin\circ e_2) &\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{WF}(e_1)\land\operatorname{WF}(e_2),\\ \operatorname{WF}(\operatorname{op}(e)) &\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{WF}(e). \end{aligned}

Here \circ ranges over binary syntax constructors and \operatorname{op} over unary constructors; branch-domain proofs are deliberately separate.

Successful evaluation by a sound FloatLib backend encloses every real value of the expression on the input panel. The semantic translation identifies that value with the original CAS expression when the coordinate environments agree, with no condition on the expression. It writes \pi, real powers and \mathrm e as FloatLib's standard calls, whose enclosures come with their own containment theorems.

For an environment enclosure \rho(i)\in_{\!B}\operatorname{env}(i), successful evaluation satisfies

\operatorname{evalInterval}(\operatorname{env},e) =\operatorname{some}(J) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(e,\rho)\in_{\!B}J.

The admissible numerical domains depend on the backend. FloatLib's default elementary enclosures require positive logarithm panels, and its real-power call requires a positive base panel. The translation sends a square-root argument through \max(0,\cdot), so negative inputs follow Mathlib's \sqrt x=0 on every backend. CEGA's certified contexts use FloatLib's total elementary table, which also treats strictly negative logarithm panels through \log x=\log|x| and the singleton zero through \log0=0. A nontrivial panel touching zero has no finite logarithm range. Division needs a denominator interval that excludes zero, or the checked lower bound below; unsupported or failed operations return none.

A checked denominator entry stores a positive rational lower bound \delta, its direct theorem \delta\leq|\operatorname{eval}(d,\rho)| on the chart, and route provenance. A certified context then evaluates the quotient a/d as a\cdot w for a fresh variable w=d^{-1} with the interval [-1/\delta,1/\delta], with the same enclosure conclusion.

Proof for Theorem 10.41
uses 0

FloatLib proves containment by induction on its expression tree: leaves use the environment and constant contracts, each operation uses the backend's soundness theorem on the inductive enclosures, and each standard call uses the containment theorem of its registered enclosure. Compose this result with the CAS translation's real-denotation equality. The lowered quotient has the value of the original one because a/d=a\cdot d^{-1} in \mathbb R, and \delta\leq|d| gives |d^{-1}|\leq1/\delta, so the fresh variable lies in its interval at every chart point. Failed operations propagate none, so every successful branch retains its containment proof.

Proof for Theorem 10.42
uses 0

Apply the backend membership theorem pointwise to obtain the real lower and upper inequalities. If those endpoints lie in [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon], transitivity gives -\varepsilon\leq f(x)\leq\varepsilon, which is equivalent to the required absolute residual bound.

How FloatLib encloses elementary functions.

An interval for f(I) must contain f(x) for every real x\in I, including irrational inputs. FloatLib's ContainsReal theorems make exactly this claim. PDEAtlas's elementary-function adapters call the upstream routines, express their results in CEGA's ordered interval interface, and connect the routines' domains to Mathlib's total real functions. The numerical series, remainder estimates, period reduction, and integer square root live in FloatLib.

Exponential enclosure. expRangeWith I order calls FloatLib's expBounds with degree d=\max(\mathrm{order},1). For an endpoint q, FloatLib chooses a binary scale s so that r=q/2^s has |r|<1. With n=d+1, its exact rational Taylor sum and error bound are

T_n(r)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{r^k}{k!},\qquad R_n(r)=\frac{|r|^n(n+1)}{n!\,n}.

The proved estimate puts \exp r in [T_n(r)-R_n(r),T_n(r)+R_n(r)]. Repeated interval squaring then uses \exp q=(\exp r)^{2^s} to restore the original scale. Monotonicity combines the lower endpoint enclosure at I.lo with the upper endpoint enclosure at I.hi, and expBounds clamps the lower bound to zero.

Logarithm enclosure. logRangeWith takes a proof that the input panel is strictly positive and calls FloatLib's logBounds?. For a positive endpoint q\geq1, binary reduction writes q=2^k r with 1\leq r<2; for 0<q<1, FloatLib first encloses \log(q^{-1}) and negates the result. The transformed series argument t=(r-1)/(r+1) lies in [0,1/3), while the separate enclosure of \log2 uses t=1/3. Writing P_d(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}t^j/j, the identity \log r=\log(1+t)-\log(1-t) gives the rational estimate

\left|\log r-\bigl(P_d(t)-P_d(-t)\bigr)\right| \leq\frac{2|t|^{d+1}}{1-|t|}.

FloatLib restores k\log2 by interval arithmetic. There is no reduction fuel limit: the binary scale comes from the rational argument. CEGA maps a requested logTerms value to d=2\max(\mathrm{logTerms},1) for this geometric remainder bound.

Square root enclosure. For q=n/d\geq0 in lowest terms, CEGA calls FloatLib's sqrtPointBounds on q d^2=nd and divides the resulting endpoints by d. With S=2^s, the upstream integer square root r=\lfloor\sqrt{ndS^2}\rfloor gives

\sqrt q\in\left[\frac{r}{dS},\frac{r+1}{dS}\right].

Trigonometric enclosures. The base calls are FloatLib's sinBounds and cosBounds, each with degree 32. They enclose the panel midpoint and inflate that enclosure by the panel radius using |f(x)-f(m)|\leq|x-m| for f=\sin,\cos. Intersecting with [-1,1] retains the global range, including when the panel crosses an extremum. For a midpoint of magnitude above 4, FloatLib reduces by approximate full periods derived from its certified enclosure of \pi/4. The error includes both the Taylor remainder and the accumulated period uncertainty. That uncertainty grows with the number of removed periods, so a narrow input panel alone does not guarantee a sharp range at large arguments.

CEGA refines these FloatLib bounds with endpoint monotonicity and sign facts when rational branch tests justify them. For example, on a panel crossing zero inside [-\pi,\pi], cosine's lower bound comes from the two endpoint enclosures and its upper bound is 1. Those endpoint enclosures also come from FloatLib. Subdivision can sharpen a range but need not improve it strictly.

Arctangent enclosure. atanRange calls FloatLib's atanBounds with parameter 16. Oddness reduces negative inputs to nonnegative ones; reciprocation reduces inputs above one to [0,1]. On (1/2,1], the identity

\arctan q=\frac{\pi}{4}+\arctan\frac{q-1}{q+1}

leaves a series argument of magnitude at most 1/2. FloatLib bounds the arctangent series by a geometric tail and encloses \pi/4 using Machin's identity \pi/4=4\arctan(1/5)-\arctan(1/239). Monotonicity combines the endpoint enclosures into a range for the full panel.

Inverse trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. Arcsine and arccosine use FloatLib's asinBounds? and acosBounds?. CEGA clamps endpoint arguments to [-1,1], proves agreement with Mathlib's total functions, and uses their monotonicity to lift point bounds to panels. If an optional point enclosure fails, a proved global range supplies the fallback. Hyperbolic ranges call FloatLib's sinhBounds, coshBounds, and tanhBounds with the requested positive exponential degree; their containment theorems pass through the same real-membership bridge.

Example: enclosing \exp(\cos x) on [-1/10, 1/10].

A conservative hand calculation shows how enclosures compose; its Taylor order is chosen by hand.

  1. Variable range. The input panel gives x \in [-1/10, 1/10].

  2. Cosine enclosure. At center 0, \cos 0 = 1. The one-Lipschitz inflation gives \cos x \in [1 - 1/10, 1 + 1/10] = [9/10, 11/10]. Intersecting with [-1, 1] gives \cos x \in [9/10, 1].

  3. Exponential enclosure. At each endpoint q\in\{9/10,1\}, use T_8(q)=\sum_{k<8}q^k/k! and R_8(q)=q^8\,9/(8!\,8). The proved Taylor estimate gives \exp(q)\in[T_8(q)-R_8(q),T_8(q)+R_8(q)]. Monotonicity therefore encloses the composition in the exact rational interval [T_8(9/10)-R_8(9/10),T_8(1)+R_8(1)].

  4. Result. These rational endpoints and the uniform enclosure proof give the data needed for an EnclosureCert. The evaluator can instead compose FloatLib's cosine and exponential bounds through the same containment rule.

The evaluator handles composed transcendental expressions without special-case code for \exp \circ \cos. Each function's enclosure feeds into the next through the generic interval backend interface. The exact range is [\exp(\cos(1/10)),\exp(1)]; the conservative cosine step accounts for much of the excess width.

The interval evaluator's compositional structure.

Expr.toFloatLib translates CAS syntax into FloatLib.Numerics.Interval.Expr. FloatLib's Expr.eval? traverses this expression using an upstream backend:

  • Rational literals are enclosed by the backend's constant operation.

  • Variables take their intervals from the supplied coordinate environment.

  • Arithmetic and elementary nodes use FloatLib's operations and containment theorems.

  • \pi, the real power a^b and \mathrm e are FloatLib's standard calls 0, 1 and 2 (Backend.Standard.extensions). The enclosures of \pi and \mathrm e follow the configured precision, and the real power needs a base interval with a positive lower endpoint.

  • Inverse sine and cosine clamp their arguments to [-1,1], and the square root takes \max(0,\cdot) of its argument, preserving Mathlib's total functions.

The translation proves agreement of real values; numerical evaluation and its soundness theorem live upstream. Ordinary multiplication followed by addition remains two expression nodes. An application requiring fused multiply-add uses FloatLib's explicit FMA node.

CEGA evaluates with Expr.evalZero?, which adds one rule to Expr.eval?: a product with an exactly zero factor, or a quotient with an exactly zero numerator, is zero whatever the other operand is. The certified context RationalInterval.CertifiedEvalContext.eval runs this evaluation on one FloatLib backend whose elementary settings come from the precision policy. Division uses either a denominator interval excluding zero or, on a second attempt, a certified positive lower bound for the actual denominator's absolute value, through the fresh reciprocal variable w=d^{-1}. FloatLib computes the ranges of the unary operations from the intervals of their arguments, so the context needs no facts about them. A failed subevaluation propagates none. The standard calls for \pi and \mathrm e run at the precision setting 128.

Direct FloatLib execution.

FloatLib provides Backend.rational for rational endpoints, Backend.binaryGrid for integer endpoints on a specified binary grid, and Backend.ofRounding for a supplied outward rounder. The latter computes rational elementary bounds and rounds them into the chosen endpoint representation. Decoding failures, rejected domains, and unrepresentable bounds propagate as none. These are upstream types and operations.

The binaryGrid representation uses scaled integers on a binary grid; it is not an IEEE format. FloatLib's certified IEEE binary32 operations form a separate facility, and the concrete CEGA backend used by the command and tactic is rational. The generic expression translation and rounding interface can connect another backend once its operations and containment proofs are supplied.

For quadrature or a Taylor model, the numerical enclosure must refer to the same exact-real rule or polynomial as the analytic certificate. Its radius then bounds replacement by the interval midpoint, including any outward rounding. Adding that radius to the analytic remainder gives the total error. An enclosure alone supplies neither differentiability nor a quadrature remainder; CEGA's analytic theorems retain those hypotheses.

A certified enclosure.

FloatLib computes interval multiplication as the exact four-corner product. For rational panels I=[a,b] and J=[c,d] the product panel has endpoints \min(ac,ad,bc,bd) and \max(ac,ad,bc,bd), which is sharp for independent factors in every sign configuration; on x\in[-1,2], y\in[2,3] it gives [-3,6] where a symmetric magnitude bound gives [-6,6].

x\in I\ \land\ y\in J \quad\Longrightarrow\quad xy\in I\cdot J.

Proof for Theorem 10.43
uses 0

The interval product bound follows from FloatLib's multiplication theorem. To see why the four corners suffice, fix the sign of y. Multiplication by y is then monotone or antitone, so xy lies between ay and by. Each of these is a fixed factor times a value between c and d, hence lies between the two corner products with that factor. Both bounds are therefore between the minimum and the maximum of the four corners.

For a rational box B=I_1\times\cdots\times I_n with midpoint m and a function differentiable on the box, the mean value theorem in centered form gives

f(x)=f(m)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial_i f(c)\,(x_i-m_i) \qquad\text{for some }c\text{ on the segment from }m\text{ to }x,

so that f(B)\subseteq f(m)+\sum_i \partial_i f(B)\,(I_i-m_i); a coordinate whose panel is a single point contributes nothing. For a symbolic expression, the checked route first certifies analytic validity throughout the box. It encloses the midpoint value and the symbolic partial derivatives, then adds the interval products with I_i-m_i. In one dimension, if J_0 encloses f(m) and D encloses f' on I, the result is J_0+D(I-m), with width \mathrm{width}(J_0)+2\,\mathrm{radius}(I)\max(|\inf D|,|\sup D|). This can improve the natural extension without a fixed derivative sign; the midpoint error and derivative magnitude determine the gain. The companion monotonicity route works coordinatewise on the same boxes: when a partial derivative \partial_i f keeps one sign on B, every value of f lies in the hull of the enclosures of f on the two faces x_i=\min I_i and x_i=\max I_i, and one planner level nests up to n such face reductions. On [1,2]^2, direct interval substitution in xy-x gives [1,4]-[1,2]=[-1,3]. As a hand calculation, the factorization x(y-1) makes the exact range [0,2] visible; likewise, xyz-xy=xy(z-1) has exact range [0,4] on [1,2]^3. Previews rank candidate routes by width, endpoint magnitude, and route length, after any correlated hyperbolic enclosure; the selected route must still construct its certificate, with fallback on failure.

Proof for Theorem 10.49
uses 0

The box is convex, so the segment from the midpoint m to x stays in it; apply the mean value theorem to t\mapsto f(m+t(x-m)) on [0,1], whose derivative is the Fréchet derivative of f applied to x-m, that is the sum of the partial derivatives weighted by the coordinate offsets, to obtain the intermediate point c. Interval soundness of the midpoint evaluation, of each partial-derivative enclosure at c, and of the products with I_i-m_i then places f(x) in the assembled box. For the face reduction, a one-signed partial derivative makes t\mapsto f(x+t e_i) monotone on the segment across the box, so f(x) lies between the values at the two faces, hence in the hull of their enclosures.

A Precision value bundles three requests for FloatLib-backed elementary ranges and a depth for checked box refinement:

(\mathrm{expOrder},\ \mathrm{sqrtDigits},\ \mathrm{logTerms},\ \mathrm{depth}) \quad\text{with defaults}\quad(8,\ 12,\ 10,\ 2).

expOrder supplies FloatLib's exponential degree after promotion of zero to one. sqrtDigits sets the binary grid for the denominator-scaled square-root bounds. logTerms maps to FloatLib degree 2\max(\mathrm{logTerms},1). The sine, cosine, and arctangent adapters use their own fixed parameters. The configuration group (prec := n) sets the first three fields to n; (depth := n) sets the subdivision depth. An omitted policy uses the defaults.

The policy is planner data. Every range theorem holds for all parameter values, so changing the policy preserves soundness while affecting cost and potential sharpness. The final width also depends on input variation, dependence between subexpressions, and period uncertainty, any of which can dominate the error.

Mathlib's dyadic_interval tactic evaluates a real proposition over intervals with dyadic endpoints and checks the outcome in the kernel. The cega_real family adds CEGA's ranges to it: quotients, natural powers, \pi, the exponential, the logarithm, the square root, the trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, and the hyperbolic functions. A bounded dyadic interval I has rational endpoints, so it passes unchanged to a CEGA range F, and the rational interval F(I) is rounded outward to the grid 2^{-p}, where p is the tactic's prec parameter. If x\in I, then f(x) lies in the rounded interval. An unbounded argument, and a reciprocal or logarithm whose argument interval contains zero, give a range that holds for every real input: [-1,1] for sine and cosine, [0,\infty) for the exponential and the square root, and the whole line otherwise. The Taylor order of the exponential family and the series length of the logarithm are at least p/2, and the square root keeps at least p+4 binary digits. The \pi bracket and the trigonometric and inverse-trigonometric series use fixed parameters; increasing p refines their outward rounding but does not refine those underlying rational ranges.

Bare cega runs this evaluation with p=32 on a goal without free variables that its carrier and box routes do not prove, such as a conjunction, a disjunction, a negation, an interval membership or an equality of real constants.

Proof for Theorem 10.51
uses 0

The rational interval with the endpoints of I contains x, so the CEGA soundness theorem places f(x) in F(I), and outward rounding only enlarges F(I). The global ranges follow from -1\le\sin x\le 1, 0<e^x, 0\le\sqrt x, \lvert\arctan x\rvert<\pi/2\le 2 and the corresponding bounds for \arcsin, \arccos, \cosh and \tanh. Mathlib's inclusion tactic composes these one-step facts along the expression tree.

10.7.3. Taylor Models🔗

Taylor models combine a finite polynomial with a uniform remainder theorem on an explicit interval. We keep three errors distinct: analytic truncation, uncertainty in the polynomial coefficients, and any roundoff used to evaluate the polynomial. A final certificate may add them, and each is bounded by its own theorem.

We return to the rational function used in the interval-enclosure figure. Subdivision narrowed the input intervals; a retained polynomial keeps algebraic dependence that a single interval would discard. The remainder panel uses its own vertical scale, making the difference visible even where the function and polynomial nearly coincide. A model needs a uniform bound on that difference throughout the stated interval; agreement at sampled points alone cannot supply it.

Uniform approximation of values does not by itself certify derivatives. For \varepsilon>0 and k>0, the smooth error e(x)=\varepsilon\sin(kx) obeys |e(x)|\leq\varepsilon, while |e'(0)|=\varepsilon k can be as large as we choose. Consequently, differentiating the polynomial in a model does not automatically give an equally accurate model of the derivative. For a PDE residual involving derivatives, we need certificates for those derivatives or a direct residual certificate, with the analytic regularity needed to interpret them. The derivative-bound and symbolic-calculus results supply these alongside the value models.

A concrete polynomial and remainder for the exponential.

FloatLib's small-argument exponential theorem gives a direct example of analytic truncation. For a rational q with |q|\leq1, choose a degree d\in\mathbb N and put n=d+1. Its polynomial and radius are

T_n(q)=\sum_{k<n}\frac{q^k}{k!}, \qquad R_n(q)=\frac{|q|^n\,(n+1)}{n!\,n}.

Both are exact rationals. As a hand specialization, d=2 gives n=3, T_3(q)=1+q+q^2/2, and R_3(q)=2|q|^3/9\leq2/9. The radius bounds the truncation error at rational points with |q|\leq1; the general Taylor-model constructors supply uniform approximation certificates from derivative bounds at arbitrary real inputs.

A model-approximation certificate records an original function, a reference function, model-order metadata, an error budget, and the proved uniform error estimate. Writing its source as f, its model as p, its domain as S, and its error as \varepsilon, the trusted field is

\forall x\in S,\qquad \lVert f(x)-p(x)\rVert\leq\varepsilon.

The stored order does not occur in this proposition; it is metadata. A supplied model need not be a Taylor polynomial or have a finite-dimensional representation, and such structure requires a separate construction.

For an ordinary scalar function on an ordered closed interval, we build the actual order-n Taylor polynomial from within-derivatives, prove that its evaluation is Mathlib's Taylor evaluation, and prove that its degree is at most n. Assuming C^{n+1} regularity on that interval, a bound C on the norm of the (n+1)-st within-derivative produces an ApproxCert with uniform error C(b-a)^{n+1}/n!, the conservative remainder supplied by Mathlib's mean-remainder theorem.

Finite-model approximations compose through the canonical ApproxCert calculus after projecting a ModelApproxCert to its stored certificate. If f and g are approximated on S by p and q with errors \varepsilon and \delta, respectively, then the additive rules prove

\begin{aligned} f+g&\sim_{\varepsilon+\delta}p+q,& f-g&\sim_{\varepsilon+\delta}p-q,& -f&\sim_{\varepsilon}-p. \end{aligned}

For real-valued functions, checked bounds |f(x)|\leq A and |q(x)|\leq B give the nonlinear rule

fg\sim_{A\delta+B\varepsilon}pq\qquad\text{on }S.

Here u\sim_\eta v abbreviates \forall x\in S,\ \lVert u(x)-v(x)\rVert\leq\eta. The rules act on the underlying ApproxCert; model-order metadata can be reattached afterwards.

Finite Taylor jets.

The jet uses the real coefficients c_0,\ldots,c_n to define the finite polynomial \sum_{k=0}^{n}c_k(x-a)^k. The certificate accepts a real-valued coefficient function; it does not require a rational or floating-point encoding. We prove three separate statements: exact coefficients recover the mathematical Taylor polynomial, coefficient intervals bound the perturbation of that polynomial, and a bound on the next derivative controls the analytic remainder. Only after those statements are available are their two error budgets added.

Reading a TaylorJetCert.

For order n=2 on [a,b] with a\leq b, a TaylorJetCert stores coefficients c_0,c_1,c_2, coefficient uncertainties \delta_0,\delta_1,\delta_2, and a bound C for the third within-derivative. Its model is

q(x)=c_0+c_1(x-a)+c_2(x-a)^2.

The certificate keeps the error calculation visible:

\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{coeff}} &=\delta_0+\delta_1(b-a)+\delta_2(b-a)^2,\\ E_{\mathrm{rem}} &=C\frac{(b-a)^3}{2!},\\ E_{\mathrm{jet}} &=E_{\mathrm{rem}}+E_{\mathrm{coeff}}. \end{aligned}

The coefficient inequalities prove that the exact Taylor polynomial is within E_{\mathrm{coeff}} of q. The derivative bound and ContDiffOn hypothesis prove that the source function is within E_{\mathrm{rem}} of the exact Taylor polynomial. Adding the two error bounds gives

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad |f(x)-q(x)|\leq E_{\mathrm{jet}}.

uses 0

Insert the exact Taylor polynomial between f and the stored jet q_n. The Taylor remainder theorem bounds the first difference, and the coefficient perturbation theorem bounds the second. The triangle inequality adds these two independent budgets, producing the certificate's soundness field.

Informal sizing calculation for \sin(x) on [0, \pi].

Suppose we request a piecewise model approximating \sin x to tolerance \eta = 10^{-4} on [0, \pi]. The adaptive algorithm proceeds:

  1. Initial attempt. At the root interval [0, \pi] with order n = 4, the remainder bound uses C = \max_{x \in [0,\pi]} |D^5\sin(x)| = 1. The remainder is C(\pi-0)^5/4! \approx 12.7, which exceeds \eta.

  2. First bisection. Split at \pi/2. On each half-panel of width \pi/2 \approx 1.57, the remainder is 1 \cdot (1.57)^5/24 \approx 0.39, still exceeding \eta.

  3. Further bisection. After 4 levels (panels of width \pi/16 \approx 0.196), the remainder is (0.196)^5/24 \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-5} < \eta. The analytic remainder fits the budget; leaf acceptance still needs the coefficient and validity certificates.

This calculation suggests 16 quartic panels. A RationalModelTree certificate has rational endpoints, whereas \pi is irrational. A checked implementation must first choose a rational outer interval and provide the derivative and coefficient certificates required by each leaf. The intended global guarantee would then have the form

\forall x \in [0, \pi], \qquad |\sin x - P_\tau(x)| \leq 10^{-4},

where P_\tau selects the appropriate leaf polynomial based on which subinterval contains x.

The distinction from pure interval arithmetic.

Classical interval arithmetic (Moore, 1966; Neumaier, 1990) replaces each real number by an interval [\underline{x}, \overline{x}] and propagates bounds through every arithmetic operation. Repeated occurrences are treated independently, which can overestimate the range. For example, evaluating x - x with x \in [0,1] yields [-1, 1] instead of \{0\}. This is the interval dependency problem; repeated enclosure of transformed sets also gives rise to the related wrapping effect.

Taylor models (Berz and Makino, 1998) mitigate this loss of correlation by retaining polynomial structure. Instead of an interval, each quantity is represented as a polynomial plus a remainder interval. Subtraction of correlated expressions can cancel matching polynomial parts exactly, leaving the remainder enclosure to account for the unresolved error. This is useful for PDE verification, where expressions such as \nabla u \cdot \nabla u - |\nabla u|^2 should simplify before interval evaluation.

PDEAtlas's Taylor certificates are approximation and composition theorems, assembled into piecewise models, rather than a Taylor-model arithmetic with the wrapping-control strategies of that literature.

The rational interval operations, such as expRange, logRange on strictly positive panels, RationalInterval.sin, and RationalInterval.cos, enclose the range of a function on a whole panel. A Taylor model instead retains a polynomial approximation over the panel; the symbolic Taylor constructors use interval analysis only to establish analytic-domain conditions and to bound the remainder derivative, while coefficient enclosures can separately supply the jet's coefficient-error budget.

Order selection and error decomposition.

The Taylor-jet certificate makes the three error sources explicit:

\underbrace{C \frac{(b-a)^{n+1}}{n!}}_{\text{truncation}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^n \delta_k (b-a)^k}_{\text{coefficient uncertainty}} + \underbrace{r_{\text{eval}}}_{\text{runtime roundoff}}.

The first term depends on the smoothness of the function and the panel width. The second term vanishes when exact symbolic coefficients are used (all \delta_k = 0). The third term is added separately by the numerical backend and is separate from the analytic approximation theorem.

The CEGA option expOrder (default defaultExpTaylorOrder = 8, so a reduced Taylor sum with n=9 terms) is a different order: it is the degree of the elementary exponential enclosure used by the interval evaluator, while a Taylor jet has its own polynomial order and these three error budgets.

RationalModelTree joins local approximation certificates along exact rational split points; the leaf models need not be polynomials. The leaf construction combines the checked symbolic derivative pipeline with a noncomputable Taylor polynomial. Given rational a<b, regularity through order n+1, and a proved nonnegative rational bound \lVert D^{n+1}_{[a,b]}f(x)\rVert\leq C, a successful leaf construction returns the exact Taylor model T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f with

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|f(x)-T^{[a,b]}_{n,a}f(x)\right| \leq C\frac{(b-a)^{n+1}}{n!}.

The compiler records analytic branch conditions explicitly and verifies rational cancellation and denominator conditions. Unsupported derivatives or failed interval obligations return none, so this theorem is exposed only after all required evidence has been constructed.

For each splittable coordinate x_i, the planner encloses the symbolic partial derivative and assigns the exact rational score

(b_i-a_i)\max\{|L_i|,|U_i|\}, \qquad \operatorname{eval}(\operatorname{diff}_i e,X)\subseteq[L_i,U_i].

This is an enclosure of the formal derivative expression. Its identification with an analytic partial derivative requires the separate validity hypotheses. The largest positive score selects the coordinate; if no score is positive, the widest coordinate with an unenclosed derivative is chosen. The ranking is a heuristic, and soundness comes from the checked interval enclosures used by the adaptive search.

ExprAdaptiveTaylor.panelOfRange is the analytic handoff from a proved derivative enclosure to a real Taylor model with an exact-rational error bound. Both it and the adaptive constructor adaptiveToTolerance? are noncomputable. The latter constructs a leaf of the requested order on each panel from the exact-rational enclosure of its remainder derivative. It retries rejected leaves on half-panels until the model tree meets the requested tolerance \eta or the finite search budget is exhausted. If the optional search returns a result with piecewise model P, Lean proves

\forall x\in[a,b],\qquad \left|\operatorname{eval}(e,x)-P(x)\right|\leq\eta.

Failure returns none, and success carries an ordinary ApproxOn theorem.

Proof for Theorem 10.66
uses 0

Every accepted leaf is produced from a derivative enclosure and the Taylor remainder theorem, hence carries a local model certificate. Recursive subdivision assembles these leaves with the model-tree soundness theorem. The successful search result also stores that the maximum leaf error is at most \eta; composing the two facts proves the root-domain approximation.

10.7.4. Derivative Bounds and Adaptive Search🔗

High-order quadrature and Taylor remainders require uniform bounds on the analytic derivative. Checked symbolic derivatives are identified with Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin and then enclosed panel by panel on a declared real domain.

Adaptive search consumes only these proved local bounds. It may accept a panel, subdivide it, compare two certified trees, or exhaust its depth budget. The search strategy is computational; the returned tree is useful because its root error theorem is independent of that strategy.

From x^4 to an analytic bound.

Let the symbolic expression be e(x)=x^4. Repeated checked differentiation and normalization produce the constant fourth derivative 24. The variable-independent route can evaluate that expression once, obtaining the degenerate enclosure [24,24], and reuse it on every requested panel.

The route then crosses two proof boundaries:

  1. the differentiation theorem identifies the checked symbolic expression with Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin 4;

  2. the interval theorem turns membership in [24,24] into an absolute-value upper bound.

The resulting IteratedDerivativeBounderOn proves, for every nondegenerate panel [a,b] in its declared domain and every x\in[a,b],

\left\|\operatorname{iteratedDerivWithin} 4\,(\lambda x,x^4)\,[a,b]\,x\right\|\leq24.

For the polynomial, smoothness is proved analytically, and a quadrature theorem receives that ContDiffOn proof separately from the numerical bound.

A rational example with a side condition.

For f(x)=1/(1+x) on [0,1], the fourth derivative simplifies to 24/(1+x)^5. The checked rational route also records the condition 1+x\neq0. Interval positivity proves that condition uniformly because 1\leq1+x\leq2 on the domain.

A range provider can then enclose the simplified derivative. Even a conservative enclosure such as [-24,24] is sufficient: converting it to a bound certificate yields the useful conclusion

\left\|f^{(4)}(x)\right\|\leq24 \qquad (0\leq x\leq1).

An IteratedDerivativeBounderOn n f s produces a BoundCert for \lVert f^{(n)}\rVert on every requested nondegenerate compact interval contained in s. The specialized interface stores only the scalar panel bound and its direct proof for Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin; its generic BoundCert is a derived projection. Constructors accept a panelwise Lean estimate, CEGA derivative enclosures, or any sound RealIntervalBackend. Smoothness is a separate analytic hypothesis; an enclosure of a formal derivative says nothing about differentiability of the original function.

On a set with UniqueDiffOn ℝ s, assume validity of the intermediate symbolic derivatives at levels k<n. The order-n checked derivative then denotes Mathlib's iteratedDerivWithin. This includes every nondegenerate closed interval contained in the validity domain. The linked regularity theorem uses the sufficient stronger assumption of validity through level n inclusive to prove ContDiffOn ℝ n: it establishes continuity of the final derivative by proving that derivative differentiable.

If e^{[n]} is the expression obtained by n checked symbolic derivatives, then on every admissible panel [a,b] and every x\in[a,b],

\operatorname{iteratedDerivWithin} n\,(\lambda y,\operatorname{eval}(e,y))\,[a,b]\,x =\operatorname{eval}\!\left(e^{[n]},x\right).

The rational route proposes a polynomial-gcd cancellation, checks its semantic equality through the exact normalizer, and turns generated denominator conditions into interval obligations. Exact rational hulls cover arbitrary real panels, and checked zero exclusion or an absolute lower bound discharges the nonzero conditions on the whole declared domain.

Writing the checked route as \operatorname{route}(d)=(r,S), its semantic boundary is the conditional identity

\operatorname{SideHolds}(\rho,S) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(d,\rho)=\operatorname{eval}(r,\rho).

The interval phase proves the premise uniformly on the panel.

Polynomial gcd cancellation proposes the reduced rational expression, but the exact normalizer proves the cross-multiplied identity. When the compiled derivative contains no occurrence of the interval variable, one verified evaluation at an enclosure of zero supplies the same bound on every real panel. This avoids asking a finite interval backend to represent arbitrary real endpoints for a constant expression.

Variable independence gives

x\notin\operatorname{vars}(d) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{eval}(d,\rho[x\mapsto t]) =\operatorname{eval}(d,\rho[x\mapsto0])

for every t; a single enclosure of the right-hand side is therefore valid on every requested panel.

A successful adaptive result contains a quadrature tree together with a proof that the sum of its leaf errors is at most the root tolerance. Projecting this result gives the ordinary interval-integral estimate for the tree's accumulated value.

For R:\mathrm{WithErrorAtMost}(f,a,b,\tau), the public theorem is

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

The generic depth-bounded search takes a proved local panel builder and interval integrability on every nondegenerate panel in the domain. It accepts a panel when its certificate meets the local tolerance, even at depth zero. Otherwise it bisects and gives each child half the budget if depth remains; with no depth left, it returns none. This generic definition compares real error bounds; the rational-budget interface supplies exact rational stopping comparisons.

Every successful search satisfies

\operatorname{search}(d,a,b,\tau)=\operatorname{some}(R) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left\|\int_a^b f-R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

    The two-point Gauss-Legendre rule as a panel rule of order 4, with its sharp one-panel constant 4320.

Why subdivision can improve a certificate.

For f(x)=x^5 on [0,1], the fourth derivative is 120x. The root panel may therefore receive the bound 120, while its left half receives the sharper bound 60. If the root certificate exceeds its assigned tolerance, adaptive search bisects the interval and asks the same derivative-bound object for each child.

The sharp Simpson budget on a panel of width h is C h^5/2880, where C bounds the fourth derivative. Thus the unsplit budget is 120/2880=1/24, while the two half-panel budgets are

\frac{60(1/2)^5}{2880}=\frac1{1536}, \qquad \frac{120(1/2)^5}{2880}=\frac1{768}.

Their sum is 1/512. Most of the gain comes from the fifth power of the panel width; the smaller derivative bound on the left improves it further.

In this construction, both children meet tolerance 1/384, and adding the child certificates gives an estimate with analytic error 1/512. The arithmetic that chooses to split plays no part in the proof, which uses only the two local error bounds, interval integrability, and additivity of the interval integral.

A rational-budget candidate contains a client result, an exact rational upper bound for its semantic error, and a proof relating the two. When decidable rational comparison accepts the candidate, its real error is at most the requested rational tolerance.

Precisely,

\operatorname{accepted}(c,\tau)=\mathrm{true} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{error}(c.\mathrm{cert})\leq(\tau:\mathbb R).

The quadrature specialization stores accepted local QuadratureCerts in the same backend-independent tree used by real-valued adaptive search. Local interval-integrability evidence justifies composing adjacent panel integrals. Both an over-budget root and a missing root candidate may therefore be recovered by proved child certificates, while a failed finite search returns none.

On success it returns exactly the root theorem

\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -R.\mathrm{tree}.\mathrm{value}\right|\leq(\tau:\mathbb R),

where a, b, and \tau are the input rationals cast to reals.

Competing subdivision trees for the same interval can be compared by their proved error budgets. The selector returns a tree with the minimum budget. More generally, a dependent leaf-refinement rule may propose a replacement tree at every accepted leaf; retaining the better local alternative is proved never to increase the accumulated root error. Candidate generation is untrusted.

For two root trees T_1,T_2,

\left\|\int_a^b f -\operatorname{select}(T_1,T_2).\mathrm{value}\right\| \leq\min\!\left(E(T_1),E(T_2)\right),

and leafwise improvement satisfies E(\operatorname{improve}(T))\leq E(T).

uses 0

For two complete trees, choose the one whose stored error budget is smaller; its existing soundness theorem supplies the integral estimate. For leafwise refinement, use structural induction on the original tree. At each leaf retain the original certificate or a proved-better replacement, and at each branch add the two inductive error inequalities.

A candidate family associates mesh, rule, or arithmetic-schedule keys with ordinary quadrature certificates and an executable Boolean acceptance test. The policy proves that every accepted result meets the requested tolerance. Finite search returns the first accepted key together with that theorem, or none if every candidate fails.

If finite search returns an accepted key k, its projection proves

\left\|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx -\operatorname{candidate}(k).\mathrm{value}\right\|\leq\tau.

Proof for Theorem 10.82
uses 0

Finite search returns a key only together with evidence that the family's acceptance predicate holds for that key. The policy theorem converts this evidence into the requested tolerance bound, and the candidate's stored quadrature soundness identifies the quantity being bounded. A failed search has no conclusion to prove.

Exact-rational candidate families obtain their Boolean test from rational comparison and transport the result to a real error theorem. A FloatLib enclosure of the exact rule value gives another such candidate: its certified endpoint radius bounds replacement by the midpoint, and that radius is added to the analytic error. For rounded endpoints, the radius must use their exact decoded values. The derivative enclosure must still bound the analytic derivative on the whole panel: order four supplies the Simpson remainder, and order n+1 supplies the degree-n Taylor remainder.

The common derivative object is used by the Simpson and two-point Gauss–Legendre constructors for one panel, fixed composites, planned tolerances, and adaptive subdivision. The total tolerance planner reserves part of the budget for analytic error and accepts a replacement value only when its proved numerical error fits the remainder.
